contexts.text:
Two possible meanings

At a fictional language workshop, Neda wrote “I saw her duck” on the board. One learner imagined a bird; another imagined a person lowering her head. The sentence was ambiguous because it allowed both interpretations. Neda then added another sentence to explain the situation. The extra context made the intended meaning precise.

The group compared dictionary entries instead of assuming that familiar words always had one meaning. They agreed that an accurate explanation should identify the relevant sense and give enough context. A long explanation was not necessarily a clear one: sometimes one carefully chosen example was more useful.

Observe before deciding

During an imagined group meeting, Arman noticed that one participant had folded her arms. He initially interpreted the gesture as disagreement. Before jumping to a conclusion, he listened to what she said. She supported the proposal and explained that the room felt cold.

Afterwards, the group discussed the difference between an observation and an interpretation. “Her arms were folded” described a visible action. “She opposed the idea” was an interpretation that needed more evidence. Their conclusion was not that gestures were meaningless, but that one movement, without context, could be misinterpreted.

Sorting the ingredients

For a fictional food-vocabulary activity, a class sorted ingredients into groups. Raisins went with dried fruit, while fresh raspberries went with soft fruit. Almonds were identified as nuts, basil as a herb, ginger as a spice, and lentils as pulses. The learners used the names to explain their choices rather than relying only on the colour of the food.

One learner initially confused celery with asparagus. The group compared their shapes: celery had long crisp stalks, while the asparagus was arranged as slender shoots. They then made separate labels, so the next activity could test recognition without copying the earlier arrangement.

An invented monthly record

These figures are invented for a language exercise. A club records income of 100 units and expenses of 70 units for a month. Subtracting the expenses from the income gives a surplus of 30 units. In the following month, income is 80 and expenses are 90, so there is a shortfall of 10 units instead.

The treasurer keeps a clear record of both months. The members first check the calculation, then discuss which costs were regular and which occurred only once. The exercise is about understanding a budget report and its vocabulary, rather than choosing a financial product or predicting future income.
